learning_objective: 🎯 Understand how a country trades with the rest of the world, how international payments are recorded, and how currency exchange rates are determined.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: An accounting statement that records all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world in a given year. It always balances in the accounting sense.

Current Account records trade in goods (visible), services (invisible), and unilateral transfers. Capital Account records transactions causing a change in assets/liabilities across borders (like FDI, loans, investments).
The price of one currency in terms of another (e.g., $1 = ₹83). Under a flexible system, it is determined by the market forces of demand and supply for foreign exchange.

Depreciation is a fall in currency value due to market forces (Demand/Supply). Devaluation is when the government/central bank deliberately lowers the value of its currency under a fixed exchange rate system.

fun_activity.title: ✈️ The Tourist Effect
fun_activity.instructions: If the Rupee depreciates ($1 goes from ₹75 to ₹83), Indian goods become cheaper for Americans. Exports will increase! However, your dream vacation to New York just became much more expensive because you need more Rupees to buy Dollars.

exam_tips: 📌 Balance of Trade (BoT) is just the difference between export and import of GOODS (visible items). BoP is much broader and includes services, transfers, and capital flows.
📌 An increase in foreign demand for Indian IT services will shift the supply of foreign exchange to the right, causing the Rupee to appreciate.
📌 Remember that 'Accommodating' transactions in BoP are done strictly to cover deficits or surpluses, while 'Autonomous' transactions are for profit.
quick_recap: ⭐ The Foreign Exchange Market can be spot (immediate delivery) or forward (future delivery).
⭐ Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) goes into the Capital Account, while profits earned from that FDI go into the Current Account.
⭐ Managed Floating is called 'dirty floating' because the central bank occasionally intervenes in the free market to prevent massive currency shocks.
